original_question: In the space-homogeneous Boltzmann or Landau equation with gamma + 2s < 0, can one obtain an a priori L-infinity bound for classical solutions? The paper presents this missing estimate as the key obstruction in the very soft potential case.
target_in_paper: The draft most closely matches the unnumbered open problem stated at the start of §7 ('The homogeneous problem'): in the very soft potential regime γ+2s<0, even for space-homogeneous Boltzmann/Landau equations one does not know how to obtain an a priori L^∞ estimate for the solution. The paper then sharpens this in §7.2 for the 3D Landau-Coulomb case via Conjecture 7.3.
correct_elements: Your draft correctly identifies the space-homogeneous setting, the relevant very soft regime γ+2s<0, the missing a priori L^∞ bound, and the fact that the paper treats this as the central obstruction in the very soft potential case.
missing_details: The equation should be stated explicitly as the homogeneous kinetic equation ∂_t f = Q(f,f), with f=f(t,v) independent of the space variable x.
The operator Q should be identified as either the non-cutoff Boltzmann collision operator with standard parameters (γ,s) or the Landau operator, which corresponds to the limit s=1.
The regime 'very soft potentials' should be spelled out as γ+2s<0; in the Landau case this becomes γ<−2, and the paper emphasizes the 3D Coulomb case γ=−3 as the most extreme model.
The solution class should be specified: nonnegative classical solutions on a time interval [0,T) (or globally), not merely weak solutions.

The hidden assumptions from §7 should be included: finite mass, finite energy, finite entropy, and enough decay as |v|→∞ so that the conservation laws used in the homogeneous discussion are valid for classical solutions.

The draft does not say what 'a priori' means the bound may depend on. In the paper this means dependence only on prescribed data, not on unknown future behavior of the solution; the contrast is with known conditional estimates that require extra weighted L^∞ control.

The draft does not specify whether the desired estimate is for every finite time interval [0,T] or uniform for all t≥0. The paper first poses the missing estimate in the former generic sense, then in the Landau-Coulomb discussion suggests the stronger conjectural form ||f(t)||_∞ ≤ C_d ||f_in||_∞.
The draft does not mention that this is exactly why the very soft range is excluded from the conditional regularity theorems earlier in the paper.
The nearby context in §7.2 should be reflected: once an L^∞ bound is available, further regularity is expected to follow from Schauder estimates.
No ambient ring/field or nilpotency condition is relevant here; the ambient analytic setting is (t,v)∈[0,T)×ℝ^d.
No phrase like 'for all sufficiently large m' occurs in this problem; the analogous hidden regularity clause here is 'sufficient decay as |v|→∞'.
refined_question: Let f=f(t,v)≥0 be a classical space-homogeneous solution of ∂_t f = Q(f,f) on [0,T)×ℝ^d, where Q is either the non-cutoff Boltzmann collision operator with parameters (γ,s) or the Landau operator (the case s=1), and assume the potential is very soft, i.e. γ+2s<0 (so, for Landau, γ<−2). If the initial data have finite mass, finite energy, finite entropy, and enough decay as |v|→∞ to justify the homogeneous conservation laws for classical solutions, can one obtain an unconditional a priori L^∞_v bound for f on every finite time interval [0,T] from prescribed data alone?
justification: I did not replace your draft by Conjecture 7.3 itself, because your wording targets the broader open problem announced at the beginning of §7: the missing a priori L^∞ estimate for homogeneous Boltzmann/Landau solutions in the full very soft regime γ+2s<0. Conjecture 7.3 is a narrower and stronger specialization to the 3D Landau-Coulomb equation. The surrounding context confirms this reading: §1 says there are presently no upper bounds in the very soft case even for space-homogeneous solutions; Theorems 3.1 and 3.2 exclude the very soft range; §7 then states that the issue is precisely the lack of an a priori L^∞ estimate when γ+2s<0; and §7.2 explains that, if one had such an L^∞ bound, further regularity would follow by standard Schauder estimates.
